name: Screen time / blue light reduction

lead: Reducing screens or blue light is said to ease eye strain and tired-looking eyes.
Trials of blue-blocking lenses mostly found no help for eye strain, and no study links this to appearance.

paras: Breaks reduce sustained near focus; filters aim to cut blue wavelengths from screens.
Low risk. The main cost is time or the price of filter lenses.

lead: Reducing screen time or blue light exposure, through breaks, filter glasses or night modes, is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to ease eye strain and the tired look around the eyes. Computer vision syndrome describes eye strain, dryness, headache and blurred vision after prolonged screen use.[1]

Randomised trials of blue-blocking lenses have mostly not found benefit for digital eye strain, and no studies were found linking screen time or blue light reduction to dark circles or other facial appearance.[1]

paras: Symptoms of computer vision syndrome include eye strain, dry or irritated eyes, headaches, blurred vision and neck pain, made worse by glare, dim surroundings and poor posture.[1] The 20-20-20 rule advises looking about 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, though the source notes no study specifically testing it.[1]

A 2007 study of 36 people found amber lenses improved irritation and tiredness, but a 2008 follow-up could not reproduce this.[1] A 2020 double-blind trial and a 2021 trial found no evidence that blue-blocking filters help digital eye strain.[1] A 2017 trial of macular carotenoid supplements reported fewer headaches and eye fatigue in heavy screen users.[1]
No studies found on screen-time or blue-light reduction and facial appearance. Studies on digital eye strain are summarised above.[1]
